Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content: If \((M,d)\) is complete, then for any nested sequence of nonempty closed sets \(F_n\) with \(\operatorname{diam}F_n\to0\) there exist points \(x_n\in F_n\) such that \(d(x_n,x_m)\le\operatorname{diam}F_n\) for every \(m>n\), the sequence \((x_n)\) is Cauchy, it converges to some \(x\in M\), and the closedness of \(F_n\) forces \(x\in F_n\) for every \(n\), which gives the first direction. Conversely, if every nested sequence of nonempty closed sets with diameters tending to 0 has nonempty intersection, then for any Cauchy sequence \((x_n)\) in \(M\) the sets \(F_n\), defined as the closures of the tails \(\{x_k\mid k\ge n\}\), are nonempty, closed, nested, and satisfy \(\operatorname{diam}F_n\le\sup_{k,l\ge n} d(x_k,x_l)\), with these suprema tending to 0, so their intersection contains a point \(x\), and \(d(x,x_n)\le\operatorname{diam}F_n\), with \(\operatorname{diam}F_n\) tending to 0, which gives \(x_n\to x\) in \(M\) and the second direction. Does this establish the equivalence?
